chapter_theme: Civakan's last war: the hero, as an ascetic, destroys the passions and the four destroying karmas with the arrows of meditation, attains omniscience, and the gods, kings and nuns come and sing hymns to the Lord.

cast.role: the hero, now a Jain ascetic who conquers his inner foes
the four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors
the gods who worship the Lord
the Vidyadhara kings who come to worship
kings of the earth who come to worship
the god, Civakan's friend from earlier, who dances
the congregation that sings the hymn to the Lord
the nuns of penance who join the hymn

3074.reading: The hero besieges the great walled fort of his foes, with knowledge as his chariot, protecting life as his horses, thought as his rutting elephant, mercy as armour, virtue as a flawless sword and the true things as the golden discs.
3074.nuance: The whole passage, 3074 to 3082, is an allegory: the army is the ascetic's virtues, the foes are the passions and the karmas that bind. The text does not say so in a plain sentence, it simply lets the war language carry it; the siege is a siege of karma.
3074.event: Civakan lays siege to the fortress of his enemies, armed with the inner qualities named as an army.

claims.claim: knowledge, protection of life, mercy and virtue are the weapons and armour with which the self conquers its enemies

3075.reading: Sleep as a rutting elephant, food as a firm chariot, forgetfulness as a flood of horses, and disease as foot-soldiers come against him; he kills them and the sea-like host of bad thought, which had come in at the gate, is shaken.
3075.nuance: The four-fold army of the foe mirrors the king's own army of 3074: elephant, chariot, horse, foot; the epic fits the ascetic's war to the shape of the royal war it has told many times before.
3075.event: The enemy host of sleep, appetite, forgetfulness and disease, with the thoughts that let them in, is broken in battle.

claims.claim: sleep, appetite and heedlessness are enemies of the ascetic to be destroyed

3076.reading: Seven and sixteen of the foes fall, eight are trampled by elephants, the neuter, the woman and the sick are named with the six 'astringent' things, and all are swallowed in the whirl of the thought named 'pity'.
3076.nuance: The numbers (seven, sixteen, eight) and the neuter, woman and sickness read as the Jain lists of the lesser passions and the three sexes of desire; this is my reading of a list the verse names without saying what it counts, and the half-lines are corrupt in places.
3076.event: Groups of the enemy fall in the field one after another.

claims.claim: the passions, in their several kinds, are destroyed one by one in the field of the mind

3077.reading: With the sons and the minister of the king named 'delusion' fallen, the bow of the Veda-desires shoots a rain of arrows, but he wards it off with the spear called 'impurity' and quickly takes the king's life with the sword of dislike.
3077.nuance: Line 2 has a full stop in the middle and a corrupt word division. மயக்கப்போர் மன்னன் is the king of confusion (the delusion-karma), and வேத here is the three drives of sex, not the scripture; this is the Jain use, and the verse leaves it for the reader to know.
3077.event: Civakan kills the king Delusion after his sons and minister have fallen.

claims.claim: delusion is the king of the enemies; the three desires (vedam) are its bow, and dislike and the contemplation of impurity are what defeat it

3078.reading: As a hunter cuts the sugarcane, as a physician cuts out a disease with medicine, he cuts the enemies limb from limb and throws a weapon against the three guests.
3078.nuance: The simile of a physician who kills the disease is the verse's own account of what the cutting is: not cruelty but cure. The three that remain are unnamed here and the rest of the passage does not say what they are.
3078.event: Civakan cuts down his enemies and turns on the remaining three.

3079.reading: As the spirit leaves a body and the blood dries within the wound, the lives of the foes pour away in a blink and fall; Death, in a garland of kuvalai, seems to drink their lives, and he is angry.
3079.nuance: The image of Death garlanded with flowers and drinking lives makes the ascetic himself Death to the karmas; it is the opposite of the Jain horror at killing a living being, and the verse can use it only because the foes are not living things.
3079.event: The enemies' lives leave them at once as Civakan strikes.

3080.reading: The four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, rise against him and point at him with their fingers; the hero kills one, Nirodhanai, with an arrow, and Pride and the rest fall to the spear called 'Viraagam', each of them dying in anger.
3080.nuance: Kural 360 names three roots of all pain (desire, anger, confusion); here the Jain list is of four (anger, pride, deceit, greed), the same four that the Jain tradition calls the kasayas. The text gives the spear its name only in the single word விராகு, which I read as the Sanskrit-derived 'virāga', dispassion.
3080.event: Civakan kills the four passions in turn, with arrow and spear.

claims.claim: anger, pride, deceit and greed are the four passions to be destroyed, the last by dispassion

3081.reading: Like the sea his lesser foes rise in a mist of petty learning, and the feeble lords who stand between knowledge, sight and attainment cannot hold; he fires the arrow named the pure meditation, like a roar of blazing fire, and they fall and are surrounded by his foot-soldiers.
3081.nuance: சுக்கிலத் தியானம் is the named Jain 'white' meditation, the last of the four meditations; the verse gives it as a weapon. The 'feeble lords of knowledge, sight and attainment' are the obstructing karmas, which I read from the Jain scheme rather than from the verse.
3081.event: Civakan fires the arrow of pure meditation and the remaining foes fall.

claims.claim: the highest meditation, the pure white meditation (sukla dhyana), destroys the last of the binding karmas

3082.reading: When the four destroying kings have fallen, he sprouts like the sun at the world's summit, the fire of his arrows spreading, swallows the three worlds and then the world of non-world, and lifts the banner of the fourfold infinite, taking sovereignty.
3082.nuance: காதிப்போர் மன்னர் are the four ghati karmas, those that obscure knowledge, sight, bliss and power; the verse's 'fourfold' (நான்மை) is the four infinites listed in 2847. The second line is difficult and I read it as the sun rising from the world's top; it is the moment the work calls attaining the supreme knowledge.
3082.event: Civakan destroys the four destroying karmas and attains omniscience, taking sovereignty over the three worlds.

claims.claim: when the four destroying karmas fall, the soul knows all three worlds and the non-world (aloka) and holds the four infinites

3083.reading: The gods in the golden world beat the drums that roar, bringing elephants, chariots, horses, lions, peacocks and nagas, and take their place in the temple of the lord's feet.
3083.event: The gods bring their mounts and gather at the Lord's temple to worship.

3084.reading: Vidyadhara kings and kings of the earth come, as swans spread their wings, bearing fragrant flowers, garlands, sandal, and bright water from dark clouds, and the heavenly wishing-tree garlands.
3084.event: The Vidyadhara and earth kings arrive with offerings.

3085.reading: Like the sun falling from the sky to take the earth, the god Sudanjanan scatters a rain of gold and flowers, blesses, shows endless dances to make the Indras marvel, and is glad, his body full of eyes.
3085.nuance: Sudanjanan is the god who in earlier ilampakams had been the yaksha rescued by Civakan and acted as his friend and helper; the verse does not say so and the reader must carry that from earlier. The body of eyes is my reading of கண் முழுது உடம்பிற் றோன்றி.
3085.event: The god Sudanjanan, once Civakan's friend, rains gold and dances before the Lord.

3086.reading: The golden seat comes with the umbrella shining like a jewelled canopy, the fans flowing like moonlight; the seat that pours its brightness is reached.
3086.nuance: The umbrella, fans and seat are the royal insignia given to the Arhat; the preacher is thus given the royal regalia of the king that he put off, which the verse accepts without comment.
3086.event: The Lord's golden seat, with umbrella and fans, is set up in the assembly.

3087.reading: The scent of his jewelled hair, of the gods' incense and the Kalpaka garland that had wandered away is surpassed by the scent of the one who cut the deeds that could not be cut; if the royal ... does not tell it, who will?
3087.nuance: The last line is corrupt, the word அரசுவா is not a word I can read, and the sense of the closing rhetorical question is a guess.
3087.event: The scent of the Lord's body surpasses all heavenly perfumes.

3088.reading: The Lord's shining teeth, coral lips and the sound of his voice outshine the Mandara tree; his scent is known as that of the one who hates the deeds, and the green-eyed one (a lion or elephant) of the golden hill cannot say it.
3088.nuance: The last line names a 'green-eyed great one' (பைங்கண்மா) whom I read as a beast of the golden mountain; the sense is the rhetorical question again, that even the best of beasts cannot speak of it.
3088.event: The splendour of the Lord's body is praised above the heavenly trees.

3089.reading: His whole body gives out light too bright to perceive, like a hill made of the sun and the moon gathered in; he who shook off the two deeds can be described, but is not the dark iron in a blazing fire black no longer?
3089.nuance: The last line is difficult. கறுப்பொழிந்த ... கரியன்றே I read as the comparison of iron which has lost its black in the fire; if so the Lord's colour is the glow of burnt-out karma.
3089.event: The Lord's body is shown shining beyond description.

claims.claim: one who has shed the two kinds of deed shines with a light no eye can take in

3090.reading: The flowers that the gods rain down, the coloured sandal, the flower dust, the pindi garlands and the incense that shows the colour of dark clouds fill the quarters with scent, and the gods wear the Lord's fragrance on their crowns.
3090.event: The gods rain flowers and perfumes and wear the Lord's fragrance on their heads.

3091.reading: The worshippers, with the god who bears the fish banner and Death slain, give up all other thought, pray 'let our birth end', and wearing flowers, sweeping the floor with sandal, worship the feet of the Lord of the path of renunciation with incense.
3091.nuance: சுறவுக்கொடிக் கடவுள் is Kaman, the god of desire whose banner is the fish; the Lord is praised for having destroyed him and Death, which makes the Arhat's victory a defeat of desire and mortality together. The verse is in a different metre from those before it, and 3091 to 3097 read as the worshippers' hymn.
3091.event: The worshippers pray for the end of birth and worship the Lord's feet.

claims.claim: the Lord of renunciation destroyed Desire and Death, and worship of his feet is for the end of births

3092.reading: We worship the Lord who cut the four deeds at once, whose pure thought blazes, who knew the three times together, and whose feet are flowers, ends the four-fold ...
3092.nuance: Here the hymn first speaks as 'we' (தொழுதும் யாம்), a change of voice from the narrator of 3074 to 3091; I read the speaker as the congregation of worshippers. The line 'நான்மைவரம்பாகி' I read as 'become the limit of the fourfold', the four infinites.
3092.event: A hymn in the first person praises the Lord's feet.

claims.claim: the Lord cut the four destroying karmas together and knows the three times

3093.reading: Like the sun risen from the roaring sea, you rose against the wailing deeds, swallowing the three worlds without casting them out, the seed of qualities, and we praise your faultless feet.
3093.nuance: The 'swallowing the three worlds' repeats the image of 3082, now as praise: where the narrator told it as a victory, the hymn tells it as a quality of the Lord.
3093.event: The worshippers praise the Lord for having risen like the sun over the deeds.

claims.claim: the Lord knows the three worlds without being stained by them, sowing qualities in himself

3094.reading: The gods stand and worship the Lord, praising him with tongues that grow numb, and the nuns of penance come and sing hymns to wash off the dust of the eyes, praising the one who has left the unpraiseable qualities beyond limit.
3094.nuance: The nuns of penance appear here in the same assembly as the gods; the verse gives women a place in the hymn of the Lord, which earlier ilampakams had also done by sending the queens to the nun's life.
3094.event: Gods and nuns praise the Lord with hymns.

3095.reading: Worship of the Lord's lotus feet, with no doubt that the doer of penance gets the deed's fruit, and the speaker salutes with pure flowers, 'the king who spoke of the true world'.
3095.nuance: The line 'செய்தவனே வினை சேரும் அதற்கு' reads as 'the doer is reached by the deed for it'; the whole verse is a salutation closing in the form of a later benediction, and its metre differs from the narrative verses.
3095.event: A worshipper salutes the Lord's feet and states the law of deeds.

claims.claim: the doer of the deed receives its fruit, without doubt

3096.reading: The petty lords who seek out only the unsound as good, and speak what is not good, have borne the mother who bears many deeds; speak, Sugata, of what they say.
3096.nuance: சுகதா (Sugata) is a name the Buddhists use for the Buddha; here a Jain hymn addresses it to the Lord, and either the title is common to all the teachers who have reached release or the verse is borrowed. The line 'பல்வினைக்கும்முலைத் தாய்பயந்தாரவர்' is difficult.
3096.event: A worshipper asks the Lord to speak against the false teachers.

claims.claim: teachers who speak what is not good are mothers who give birth to many deeds

3097.reading: Having praised the feet of the one whose virtue the mind cannot know, those who worship the unbroken praise bow, filled like a treasure house, so that the heroes know the fate that does not fall.
3097.nuance: The last verse of the ilampakam as numbered here closes in praise; the grammar of the last two lines is hard and I give only the gist.
3097.event: The worshippers conclude their praise and bow.

links.note: 2845 gives knowledge, faith and conduct as the three that make release; 3074 turns knowledge into the chariot, mercy into armour and virtue into the sword.
links.teaches: The ilampakam's plain teaching of the three jewels is here made into an army, so the reader sees what the three do and not only that they are three.

links.note: 2819 makes virtue (sila) the armour of warring kings; in 3074 mercy is the armour and sila the sword.
links.teaches: The same virtue moves from a guard to a weapon, showing that in this ascetic war sila both protects and wins.

links.note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3082 shows the fire's end: the four destroying kings fall and the three worlds are known.
links.teaches: A teaching that the three burn deeds is fulfilled in the hero's own omniscience, so the doctrine is shown as an event in a life.

links.note: 2847 lists the four infinites of the liberated, and 3082 lifts the banner of the fourfold infinite.
links.teaches: The list of what release gives is shown as something one person takes, with the world swallowed, and not only a catalogue.

links.note: 3082 has Civakan win omniscience by his own war on the karmas; Tirumanthiram 113 has the Lord come down in a body, set his feet on the devotee's head and cut away the stain.
links.teaches: One text has the soul win release by its own battle, the other has it given from above, so the two disagree on whose act cuts the deeds.

gains.a: the war of the passions is set against a release that is given and not fought for, so its self-reliance becomes a choice
gains.b: the grace that cuts the stain is set beside a release won by effort, so its giver is seen to be what the Jain refuses

links.note: 3093 repeats 3082's swallowing of the three worlds, there as the narrator's victory, here as praise in the worshippers' mouths.
links.teaches: The same image is first an event and then a creed, and the hymn shows how a story becomes what a community says.

links.note: Kural 360 names three roots of pain, desire, anger and confusion; 3080 names four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors who must be slain.
links.teaches: The Jain list of four widens the Kural's three, showing that one counts the roots of pain differently depending on the school.

gains.a: the four passions, as warriors, get a rule that when their very names perish pain perishes
gains.b: the Kural's three roots get a fourth and a fighting form: pride and deceit, and a weapon against them

links.note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 3091 prays 'let our birth end' to the Lord who destroyed Desire and Death.
links.teaches: The Kural says the feet carry across, and the verse names who the Lord has beaten (Desire and Death) and why they should be prayed to.

gains.a: the prayer for the end of birth is given a wider rule that reaching his feet is the way to cross
gains.b: the Kural's Lord, who is left unnamed, is shown as one who has killed Desire and Death

links.note: Kural 9 praises the one of eight qualities; 3092 praises the one who has cut four deeds together and knows the three times.
links.teaches: One text counts a Lord by eight qualities and the other by four deeds cut, so the reader sees two different measures of the same worshipped figure.

gains.a: a Lord counted by four destroyed karmas is seen beside a Lord counted by eight qualities
gains.b: the Kural's eight qualities, left unnamed, can be compared with a Jain account of what is cut and known

links.note: 3082 tells the cutting of the four destroying karmas and the knowing of the three worlds; 3092 sings it as the Lord's own deed.
links.teaches: The event of 3082 becomes the praise of 3092, so the narrator's story is shown as the hymn's ground.

links.note: 3081 fires the arrow of pure meditation like a roaring fire to destroy the foes; Tirumanthiram 219 has deeds burnt by the fire that is worshipped and fed with ghee.
links.teaches: One text burns deeds by an inner meditation like fire, the other by an outer fire kindled in worship, so the two disagree on where the fire is.

gains.a: the meditation that burns is seen as an inner fire beside the Saiva fire kindled in ritual
gains.b: the ritual fire that burns deeds is set beside a Jain fire that burns them with no offering

source_issues: Stanzas 3074-3086 and 3088-3090 print in 8 half-lines in the edition and have been joined into 4 lines.
3077 line 2 has a stray full stop inside the line.
3087 line 4 contains அரசுவா, which I cannot read; the stanza may be corrupt.
3091-3097 are in a different, shorter metre from the verses before them; 3095-3097 read as a closing benediction and may be a later addition or a separate hymn.
